opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things that I think gets overlooked when people talk about AI agents speeding up research or other kinds of work. The naive picture is: the AI can do a task ten times faster than a human, so you get a tenfold speedup. But a lot of the time the bottleneck isn't how fast the work gets done; it's the human in the loop.

Suppose you hand off a task to an AI system and it finishes in twenty minutes rather than the two days it would have taken you. That's great, but if you then need to look at the result, decide what to do next, and give it the next instruction, the whole pipeline is gated on you being awake and at your desk. Humans sleep about a third of the day. We also take evenings off, weekends, holidays, and we spend a lot of the working day in meetings or answering email. So the fraction of the week in which a given person is actually available to review output and redirect an agent might be something like a quarter, maybe less.

That means even if the AI were infinitely fast, if every step needed a human check-in, you'd be capped at a modest multiple of your current speed, because the AI would just sit idle waiting for you to wake up. It's a bit like Amdahl's law in computing: if a portion of the process can't be sped up, that portion comes to dominate the total time.

There are a few ways around it, and they're quite revealing. One is to give the AI longer, more autonomous tasks, so it can work through the night without needing you. But that depends on how long a task these systems can reliably complete on their own, and how much you trust them to do it without supervision. Another is to hand the oversight role itself to AI systems, to have AIs checking AIs. And a third is to restructure teams so there's always someone awake, a kind of follow-the-sun model across time zones.

But each of those involves removing humans from the loop to some degree, and I think that's the important point. The very large speedups people sometimes talk about don't come for free. They come from reducing human oversight. So when someone says AI will make research a hundred times faster, it's worth asking what that implies about how much humans are still involved in steering it. The speedup and the loss of oversight are often two sides of the same coin.

r001.rationale: The response says human sleep limits when a person can review and redirect AI work, but does not address whether AI acceleration gives the person more overnight mental processing.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that mental processing during sleep may help produce scientific breakthroughs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's actually one of the things I find most striking when I think about this carefully. If you imagine a human researcher, they're only working maybe eight hours a day, five days a week. Then you subtract sleep, weekends, holidays, time with family, time eating — all of that. So out of the 168 hours in a week, a person might be doing genuinely productive cognitive work for something like 40 of them, and realistically it's often less than that if you're honest about it.

Now an AI system doesn't have any of those constraints. It doesn't sleep, it doesn't take weekends, it doesn't get tired at four in the afternoon. So even before you get to the question of whether the AI is smarter or thinks faster than a human, there's this very mundane factor of roughly a four-fold difference just from being able to run around the clock. And that's quite separate from the parallelism — the fact that you can run many copies at once — or the raw speed of inference.

But the thing I'd want to stress is that this cuts both ways when you're thinking about how much AI can speed up human work. If the bottleneck is a human who needs to review things, make decisions, give direction, then the human's limits get reimposed on the whole process. You can have an AI that produces a hundred drafts overnight, but if a person still has to read them all the next morning, the human's waking hours become the constraint again. So the speedup you get in practice depends enormously on how much of the loop still runs through a person.

I think people sometimes get this wrong in both directions. Some imagine the speedup is basically unlimited because the AI never stops, and others assume it's modest because the human is always in the loop. The real question is which tasks you can take the human out of entirely, and which ones you can't or shouldn't. And for the ones where you can't, the human's need for sleep and rest and a life outside work is a pretty hard ceiling. I don't think that's a bad thing, either. It's one of the places where the pace of change gets naturally throttled to something closer to what people can actually absorb.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can produce work overnight, but a person who must review or direct it is still limited by waking hours and sleep, so AI does not proportionally increase that person’s overnight mental processing.

r002.rationale: The response discusses sleep as a limit on human work but does not suggest that mental processing during sleep may help produce scientific breakthroughs.

astra-6.text:
Well, one thing that matters is whether the human has to remain in the loop. Suppose an AI can do a task in a few minutes that would have taken you a day, but then it needs you to look at the result and tell it what to do next. If you’ve gone to bed, it may spend the next eight hours waiting for you. Making it another hundred times faster doesn’t really help with that delay.

So there’s a distinction between speeding up individual tasks and speeding up the whole process. If the process alternates between AI work and human decisions, the human parts can become the bottleneck very quickly. And that includes time when we’re asleep or away for the weekend, as well as the time we actually spend thinking about the results.

You could address some of this by having people working in shifts. But the larger change would come if the AI could carry on through those intermediate steps itself—assessing its results, deciding what to try next, and doing that without waiting for us. Then it could make substantial progress while we’re asleep. How much autonomy it has, and how often it needs human input, could therefore matter just as much as how fast it performs each task.

r001.rationale: The response says a faster AI cannot overcome the delay when it needs a human who is asleep to review results, so task speedups do not translate proportionally into faster progress overnight.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI working autonomously while people sleep, but does not say that human mental processing during sleep can help produce scientific breakthroughs.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, one useful way to think about this is to imagine that the work itself became almost instantaneous. You’d still have to ask for it, look at the result, decide what to do next, and so on. And if the result comes back just after you’ve gone to bed, it may sit there for eight hours before anything happens.

So there’s a distinction between speeding up a particular task and speeding up the whole process. If AI makes something that used to take a day take a minute, that’s an enormous improvement in the task. But if you only check in once a day, the overall process might still move at roughly the same pace.

You can get around some of that by giving the AI more autonomy, so it can keep working through those intermediate steps while you’re asleep or away. But then the question becomes how much it can do before it needs your judgement again. The remaining human decisions can become bottlenecks, even if they’re quite a small fraction of the work.

r001.rationale: It says results may wait until morning and that human check-ins can bottleneck the process, but does not state that acceleration fails to give a person proportionally more mental processing overnight.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that mental processing during sleep helps produce scientific breakthroughs.
